l: Assyria, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: The Assyrian will fall by a sword not of man or mankind, which will devour him. He will flee, his young men will become subject to forced labor, and his rock will pass away in terror while his princes fear the banner.

l: those who help Egypt (reliance on Egypt), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 31
s: Those who go down to Egypt for help, trusting in many horses, chariots, and strong horsemen, are met with woe because they do not look to the Holy One of Israel or seek the LORD. The LORD will rise against the help of those who work iniquity, so that the helper stumbles, the helped falls, and all are consumed together.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: Chapter 32 opens with a promise that a king will reign in righteousness and princes in justice, with a man serving as shelter from wind and storm. Perception and speech will be restored, and the fool and scoundrel, who speak folly, plot iniquity and use lying words to destroy the humble and deprive the hungry and thirsty, will no longer be honored, while the noble devises noble things. The prophet then addresses the women at ease, warning them to tremble because the vintage will fail, the harvest won't come, and thorns and briers will overrun my people's land and the joyous city, leaving the palace and city deserted and turned into dens for wild donkeys and pasture for flocks. This desolation lasts until the Spirit is poured on us from on high, when the wilderness becomes a fruitful field and justice and righteousness dwell there, bringing peace, quietness and confidence forever. My people will live in peaceful habitations even though hail flattens the forest and the city is leveled, and those who sow beside all waters are called blessed.

l: righteous king (throne in the tent of David), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: A king is promised who will reign in righteousness, alongside princes who rule in justice. This opens the chapter's vision of a just order.

l: fool, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The fool will no longer be called noble. He speaks folly, works iniquity in his heart, practices profanity, utters error against the LORD, and empties the soul of the hungry and makes the thirsty's drink fail.

l: scoundrel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The scoundrel will no longer be highly respected. His ways are evil, and he devises wicked plans to destroy the humble with lying words, even when the needy speaks right.

l: noble, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The noble devises noble things and will continue in noble things. This stands in contrast to the fool and the scoundrel.

l: women at ease, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The women who are at ease, also called careless daughters, are told to rise, hear, and tremble. They are to strip themselves, put sackcloth on their waists, and beat their breasts for the pleasant fields and fruitful vine, because they will be troubled for days beyond a year.

l: my people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: Thorns and briers will come up on my people's land. After the desolation, they will live in a peaceful habitation, safe dwellings, and quiet resting places, even though hail flattens the forest and the city is leveled.

l: joyous city, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: Thorns and briers will grow on all the houses of joy in the joyous city. Its palace will be forsaken and the populous city deserted, with the hill and watchtower becoming dens forever, a delight for wild donkeys and a pasture of flocks.

l: Spirit, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The desolation will last until the Spirit is poured on us from on high. This outpouring marks the turning point at which the wilderness becomes a fruitful field.

l: wilderness, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The wilderness will become a fruitful field once the Spirit is poured out. Justice will then dwell in it.

l: fruitful field, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The fruitful field is considered a forest, and the wilderness is to become a fruitful field. Righteousness will remain in it.

l: righteousness, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: Righteousness is the basis of the king's reign and will remain in the fruitful field. Its work will be peace, and its effect quietness and confidence forever.

l: vintage and harvest failure, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 32
s: The vintage will fail and the harvest won't come, which troubles the careless women. The people are to mourn the pleasant fields and the fruitful vine.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 33
s: Chapter 33 opens with a woe against a destroyer and betrayer who will in turn be destroyed and betrayed. The people pray to the LORD for grace and strength, and the LORD declares he will now arise and be exalted, turning the plans of his opponents into chaff and stubble and burning peoples like lime and thorns. The sinners in Zion tremble at the devouring fire, and the text answers who can live with it: the one who walks righteously, speaks blamelessly, and refuses bribes and bloodshed. That person will dwell on high with secure bread and water, and will see the king in his beauty. The chapter ends with Zion pictured as a quiet, unmovable city where the LORD is judge, lawgiver, and king, enemy ships are helpless and the lame take plunder, and the inhabitants are forgiven their iniquity.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 33
s: The LORD is asked to be gracious and to be the people's strength and salvation, and is described as exalted, dwelling on high, and filling Zion with justice and righteousness. He declares that he will now arise and be exalted, bringing fire on the peoples, and calls both far and near to acknowledge his might. He is named Zion's judge, lawgiver, and king who will save, and he will be with them in majesty.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 33
s: Zion is filled by the LORD with justice and righteousness, and is the home of sinners who now fear his fire. It is pictured as the city of appointed festivals and as Jerusalem, a quiet habitation like a tent whose stakes will never be plucked up. The LORD will be with it in majesty beside wide rivers where no hostile ship can pass, and its people will be forgiven their iniquity.

l: destroyer (the one who destroys and betrays), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 33
s: The destroyer is met with a woe because he destroys and betrays though he himself was not destroyed or betrayed. When he finishes, he will be destroyed and betrayed in turn. He is also described as breaking the covenant and despising cities and man, and his rigging is later shown untied while the lame divide his plunder.

l: sinners in Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 33
s: The sinners in Zion are afraid and trembling seizes the godless among them. They ask who can live with the devouring fire and everlasting burning.

l: righteous man, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 33
s: The righteous man walks righteously, speaks blamelessly, despises gain from oppression, refuses bribes, and shuts his ears and eyes to bloodshed and evil. He will dwell on high in a fortress of rocks, with bread supplied and sure water. His eyes will see the king in his beauty and a distant land.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: Chapter 34 summons the nations and the earth to hear that the LORD is enraged against all the nations and their armies and has given them over to slaughter. The sky's army dissolves and the sky is rolled up like a scroll, and the LORD's sword, having drunk its fill in the sky, comes down on Edom for judgment. The LORD holds a sacrifice in Bozrah and a great slaughter in Edom, on a day of vengeance and a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. Edom's land becomes burning pitch and sulfur and lies waste forever, with no one passing through. Pelicans, porcupines, owls, ravens, jackals, ostriches, wolves, wild goats, the night creature, the arrow snake and kites possess it, each with its mate, by the LORD's command, lot, and measuring line.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: The LORD is enraged against all the nations and gives them over to slaughter. He holds a sacrifice in Bozrah and a day of vengeance for the cause of Zion, stretches the line of confusion and plumb line of emptiness over Edom, and by his mouth and Spirit gathers the creatures that will possess it, casting the lot and dividing the land to them with a measuring line.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: The nations and peoples are summoned to hear, along with the earth and all it contains. The LORD is enraged against them and their armies, has utterly destroyed them, and has given them over to slaughter. Their slain are cast out, a stench rises from their bodies, and the mountains melt in their blood.

l: Edom, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: Edom is the target of the LORD's sword, called the people of his curse, and suffers a great slaughter in its land, including at Bozrah. Its streams turn to pitch, its dust to sulfur, and its land to burning pitch that is not quenched night or day, and it lies waste from generation to generation with no one passing through. Its nobles and princes come to nothing, thorns and nettles overgrow its palaces and fortresses, and wild creatures possess it forever.

l: sword (the LORD's sword), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: The LORD's sword has drunk its fill in the sky and then comes down on Edom for judgment. It is filled with blood and covered with fat, the blood of lambs and goats and the fat of the kidneys of rams.

l: sacrifice (the LORD's sacrifice in Bozrah), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: The LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, accompanied by a great slaughter in the land of Edom. The sacrifice is pictured with the blood and fat of lambs, goats and rams on the LORD's sword, and wild oxen and bulls come down with them so that the land is drunk with blood and its dust made greasy with fat.

l: year of the LORD's favor and day of vengeance, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: The LORD has a day of vengeance, described also as a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. Its results are seen in the burning pitch and sulfur of Edom's land, which is never quenched and stays desolate forever.

l: desolate-land creatures (Edom's inhabitants), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 34
s: The pelican, porcupine, owl and raven possess and dwell in Edom, joined by jackals, ostriches, wolves, the wild goat, the night creature, the arrow snake and kites. Each has its mate, and none is missing, because the LORD's mouth commanded it and his Spirit gathered them. He cast the lot and divided the land to them with a measuring line, so they will possess it forever, from generation to generation.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: Chapter 35 describes the joyful transformation of the wilderness and desert, which blossom like a rose and receive the glory of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon. The people are urged to strengthen weak hands and feeble knees and to tell the fearful that their God will come with vengeance and save them. When God comes, the blind, deaf, lame and mute will be healed, and water will break out in the desert. A highway called The Holy Way will appear, closed to the unclean and to wicked fools and free of lions and ravenous animals, and the redeemed will walk on it. The LORD's ransomed ones will return to Zion singing, crowned with everlasting joy, while sorrow and sighing flee away.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: The LORD's glory and excellence will be seen, and He is called 'our God' who will come with vengeance and retribution to save the fearful. His ransomed ones are the people who return to Zion with singing.

l: wilderness (the desert land), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: The wilderness and dry land will be glad, and the desert will rejoice and blossom abundantly like a rose. It will be given the glory of Lebanon and the excellence of Carmel and Sharon. Waters and streams will break out in it, burning sand will become a pool, and the thirsty ground will become springs, with grass, reeds and rushes growing where jackals lay.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: Zion is the destination to which the LORD's ransomed ones will return with singing.

l: The Holy Way, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: A highway and road will be there and be called 'The Holy Way'. The unclean and wicked fools will not pass over it, and no lion or ravenous animal will be found on it. It is for those who walk in the Way, and the redeemed will walk there.

l: The Holy People, The LORD’s Redeemed, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: The redeemed will walk on the Holy Way. The LORD's ransomed ones will return and come to Zion with singing, with everlasting joy on their heads, and they will obtain gladness and joy as sorrow and sighing flee.

l: blind, deaf, lame and mute (the afflicted healed), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: When God comes to save, the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. The lame man will leap like a deer and the tongue of the mute will sing.

l: joy and gladness (everlasting joy replacing sorrow), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 35
s: The wilderness will rejoice with joy and singing, and the ransomed will have everlasting joy on their heads. They will obtain gladness and joy, while sorrow and sighing flee away.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria captured all the fortified cities of Judah and sent Rabshakeh with a large army from Lachish to Jerusalem. Rabshakeh stood by the aqueduct and delivered a taunting message to Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah, mocking trust in Egypt and in the LORD and claiming the LORD had told him to destroy the land. When the officials asked him to speak Aramaic rather than the Jews' language, he instead called out loudly in the Jews' language to the people on the wall, urging them not to trust Hezekiah and promising them a land of grain and wine if they surrendered. He argued that no gods of other nations, such as those of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, and Samaria, had saved their lands from Assyria. The people stayed silent as the king commanded, and the three officials returned to Hezekiah with torn clothes to report Rabshakeh's words.

l: Hezekiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Hezekiah is king of Judah in the fourteenth year of his reign, when Assyria captures Judah's fortified cities. Rabshakeh accuses him of removing the LORD's high places and altars and of deceiving the people into trusting the LORD. He commands that Rabshakeh not be answered and receives his officials' report of the Assyrian's words.

l: Sennacherib, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, attacks and captures all the fortified cities of Judah. He sends Rabshakeh with a large army from Lachish to Jerusalem, and his words are presented by Rabshakeh as those of 'the great king.'

l: Rabshakeh, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Rabshakeh is sent by the king of Assyria from Lachish to Jerusalem with a large army and stands by the aqueduct. He mocks Judah's trust in Egypt and in the LORD, claims the LORD told him to destroy the land, and refuses to speak Aramaic. He calls out in the Jews' language to the people on the wall, offering them peace and a good land if they surrender and denying that any god can deliver from Assyria.

l: Eliakim, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who is over the household, goes out to meet Rabshakeh. He asks him to speak in Aramaic so the people on the wall will not understand, then remains silent at the king's command. He returns to Hezekiah with torn clothes to report Rabshakeh's words.

l: Shebna, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Shebna the scribe goes out with Eliakim and Joah to meet Rabshakeh and joins in asking him to speak Aramaic. He stays silent as commanded and returns to Hezekiah with torn clothes to report what was said.

l: Joah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, goes out with Eliakim and Shebna to meet Rabshakeh and joins in asking him to speak Aramaic. He remains silent as commanded and returns to Hezekiah with torn clothes to report Rabshakeh's words.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Jerusalem is the city to which Rabshakeh is sent with a large army, and he stands by the aqueduct from the upper pool on the fuller's field highway. Its people sit on the wall, and Rabshakeh urges them to make peace and come out. He asks why the LORD should deliver Jerusalem when no other nation's gods saved their lands.

l: Egypt, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Rabshakeh calls Egypt a bruised reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it, and says Pharaoh is the same to all who trust him. He mocks Judah for trusting Egypt for chariots and horsemen.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Rabshakeh mocks Judah's trust in the LORD, noting that Hezekiah removed his high places and altars. He claims the LORD told him to go up against the land and destroy it, and asserts that the LORD will be unable to deliver Jerusalem, as the gods of other nations could not.

l: people on the wall (of Jerusalem), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: The people who sit on the wall are the audience Rabshakeh deliberately addresses in the Jews' language, warning that they will eat their own dung and drink their own urine. He tells them not to trust Hezekiah and promises them vines, fig trees, and a land of grain and wine if they surrender. They remain silent and give no reply, as the king commanded.

l: gods of the nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Rabshakeh cites the gods of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, and other countries, saying none delivered their lands from the king of Assyria. He also says they did not deliver Samaria, and uses this to argue that the LORD will not save Jerusalem.

l: Assyrian siege of Judah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 36
s: Assyria under Sennacherib has captured all of Judah's fortified cities and now sends a large army with Rabshakeh to Jerusalem. The unit records this confrontation as a war of words, with demands for surrender and promises of resettlement. It ends with Judah's officials reporting the threats to Hezekiah with torn clothes.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: King Hezekiah of Judah, on hearing Rabshakeh's taunts, tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and sends Eliakim, Shebna, and the priestly elders to Isaiah, who relays the LORD's promise that the Assyrian king will hear news, return home, and fall by the sword. Sennacherib, through letters carried by messengers, again insists that no god has saved any nation he has conquered, and Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD and prays for deliverance so that all kingdoms will know the LORD alone is God. Isaiah answers with the LORD's message mocking Sennacherib's arrogance, promising a sign of recovery and renewed growth for the remnant, and declaring that Assyria will not shoot an arrow at Jerusalem. The LORD's angel strikes 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp, Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer kill him with the sword in the house of his god Nisroch, after which Esar Haddon reigns in his place.

l: Hezekiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Hezekiah tears his clothes, wears sackcloth, goes to the LORD's house, and sends envoys to Isaiah asking for prayer for the remnant. After receiving Sennacherib's letter, he spreads it before the LORD and prays that the LORD save Judah so all kingdoms may know he alone is the LORD. The LORD answers through Isaiah and defends the city for his own sake and for David's sake.

l: Sennacherib, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, is warring against Libnah and sends a letter to Hezekiah claiming that the gods of conquered nations could not save them and that Jerusalem's God cannot either. The LORD denounces his pride, promises to put a hook in his nose and turn him back, and after his army is struck he returns to Nineveh. There his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer kill him with the sword while he worships in the house of Nisroch, and his son Esar Haddon reigns in his place.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Isaiah, son of Amoz, receives Hezekiah's envoys and tells them not to fear, relaying the LORD's word that the Assyrian king will hear news, return home, and fall by the sword. After Hezekiah prays, Isaiah sends the LORD's longer message condemning Sennacherib, giving a sign of recovery over three years, and promising that the city will be defended.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: The LORD, called the living God and the Holy One of Israel, promises through Isaiah to send a spirit into the Assyrian king so he hears news and returns home to die by the sword. He answers Hezekiah's prayer by declaring that he planned Assyria's conquests long ago, that he knows Sennacherib's raging, and that he will defend Jerusalem for his own sake and David's. His angel then strikes 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp.

l: Rabshakeh, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Rabshakeh is the Assyrian king's envoy whose words Hezekiah's messengers say were sent to defy the living God. He returns and finds the king warring against Libnah, having departed from Lachish. Hezekiah's envoys hope the LORD will rebuke his words.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Jerusalem is threatened by Assyria but is promised that the king of Assyria will not enter it, shoot an arrow there, come before it with a shield, or cast up a mound against it. The LORD declares he will defend the city for his own sake and for David's sake. A remnant is to go out from Jerusalem and survivors from Mount Zion, and the daughter of Jerusalem is said to shake her head at Sennacherib.

l: Assyrian army (Sennacherib's army), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: In the Assyrian camp, the LORD's angel strikes 185,000 men dead in a single night. When the men rise early in the morning, all of them are dead bodies. Sennacherib then departs and returns to Nineveh.

l: Assyrian blasphemy and threat against Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Rabshakeh's words and Sennacherib's letter say that Hezekiah's God will deceive him, that Assyria has utterly destroyed all lands, and that the gods of Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, Eden, Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah failed to save their peoples. The LORD calls this blasphemy against the Holy One of Israel and answers by promising to turn Sennacherib back. The threat ends without any arrow shot at the city.

l: Hezekiah's prayer, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 37
s: Hezekiah prays in the LORD's house, addressing him as LORD of Armies, enthroned among the cherubim, and sole God of all the kingdoms who made heaven and earth. He asks the LORD to hear Sennacherib's words, admits that Assyria destroyed nations whose gods were only wood and stone, and asks for salvation so all kingdoms may know the LORD alone. Isaiah relays that the LORD has heard this prayer and will act against Sennacherib.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: Hezekiah, king of Judah, falls sick and near death, and the prophet Isaiah tells him on the LORD's behalf to set his house in order because he will die. Hezekiah turns to the wall, prays, and weeps bitterly, and the LORD sends Isaiah back to say that He has heard the prayer and seen the tears, and will add fifteen years to Hezekiah's life and deliver him and the city from the king of Assyria. As a sign, the LORD causes the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz to go back ten steps. Hezekiah's writing then recounts his anguish at facing death, his praise for being delivered from the pit and having his sins cast behind the LORD's back, and his vow to sing in the LORD's house. The chapter closes with Isaiah's instruction to apply a cake of figs as a poultice on the boil, and Hezekiah's question about the sign that he will go up to the LORD's house.

l: Hezekiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: Hezekiah, sick and near death, is told by Isaiah that he will die, so he turns his face to the wall, prays, appeals to his faithful walk before the LORD, and weeps bitterly. The LORD grants him fifteen more years and promises to deliver him and the city from the king of Assyria. He recovers, writes a song of lament and thanks, and asks what the sign will be that he will go up to the LORD's house.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: Isaiah, the prophet and son of Amoz, delivers the LORD's message to Hezekiah that he will die and should set his house in order. He is then sent back with the LORD's reply that fifteen years will be added to Hezekiah's life. He also directs that a cake of figs be laid as a poultice on the boil so that Hezekiah will recover.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: The LORD, called the God of David Hezekiah's father, hears Hezekiah's prayer and sees his tears. He adds fifteen years to Hezekiah's life, promises to deliver him and the city from the king of Assyria, and gives a sign by making the sundial's shadow return ten steps. Hezekiah credits Him with restoring him, delivering him from the pit, and casting all his sins behind His back.

l: sundial of Ahaz, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: The sundial of Ahaz is the instrument on which the LORD causes the shadow, which had gone down with the sun, to return backward ten steps. The sun is said to have returned ten steps on this sundial.

l: Hezekiah's sickness and recovery, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: Hezekiah's illness brings him near death, and Isaiah first announces from the LORD that he will die. After his prayer the LORD reverses this, and Hezekiah recovers. A boil is mentioned, and Isaiah prescribes a poultice made from a cake of figs so that he will recover.

l: fifteen added years of life, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: The LORD promises to add fifteen years to Hezekiah's life in answer to his prayer and tears. The promise comes together with deliverance for Hezekiah and the city from the king of Assyria, and the LORD gives a sign that He will do it.

l: sign (the sundial shadow returning), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: The sign is offered by the LORD to show that He will do what He has spoken: the shadow on the sundial of Ahaz will go back ten steps. The text says the sun returned ten steps on the sundial on which it had gone down. Hezekiah separately asks what the sign is that he will go up to the LORD's house.

l: Hezekiah's writing (psalm of thanksgiving), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 38
s: The writing records Hezekiah's thoughts when he was sick and after he recovered. It describes his fear of going into the gates of Sheol, his moaning like a dove, and his anguish. It then turns to praise: the LORD has delivered him from the pit and cast his sins behind His back, the living praise Him while Sheol cannot, and Hezekiah resolves to sing with stringed instruments in the LORD's house all his days.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Merodach-baladan, king of Babylon, sends letters and a gift to Hezekiah after hearing that Hezekiah had been sick and recovered. Hezekiah is pleased and shows the Babylonian envoys everything in his house and dominion, including his silver, gold, spices, oil, and armor. The prophet Isaiah questions Hezekiah about the visitors and then delivers the word of the LORD of Armies: everything in Hezekiah's house will one day be carried to Babylon, and some of his sons will be taken to serve as eunuchs in the Babylonian king's palace. Hezekiah answers that the LORD's word is good, adding that there will be peace and truth in his own days.

l: Merodach-baladan, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan and king of Babylon, sends letters and a present to Hezekiah after hearing that Hezekiah had been sick and had recovered. His messengers are then shown all of Hezekiah's treasures.

l: Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Babylon is described by Hezekiah as a country far from him, from which the envoys came. Isaiah prophesies that Hezekiah's household treasures and some of his sons will be carried there, with the sons becoming eunuchs in the king of Babylon's palace.

l: Hezekiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Hezekiah is pleased by the letters and gift from Babylon and shows the envoys everything in his house and dominion, withholding nothing. When Isaiah questions him and announces the LORD's word of coming loss, Hezekiah calls the word good and says there will be peace and truth in his days.

l: Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Isaiah the prophet comes to Hezekiah and asks what the men said, where they came from, and what they saw. He then delivers the LORD's word that all Hezekiah's possessions and some of his sons will be taken to Babylon.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: The LORD of Armies speaks through Isaiah, declaring that the days are coming when everything in Hezekiah's house and all his fathers have stored up will be carried to Babylon, leaving nothing. He also declares that Hezekiah's sons will be taken and made eunuchs in the Babylonian king's palace.

l: envoys from Babylon (Merodach-baladan's messengers), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: The envoys bring letters and a present from Merodach-baladan to Hezekiah. Hezekiah shows them his whole house of precious things, his armor, and all his treasures, so that they have seen everything he has.

l: Hezekiah's treasures (house of precious things), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Hezekiah's treasures include silver, gold, spices, precious oil, and a house of armor, all of which he shows to the Babylonian envoys. Isaiah prophesies that all of it, along with what Hezekiah's fathers stored up, will be carried to Babylon and nothing will be left.

l: Hezekiah's descendants (sons), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: The LORD declares through Isaiah that some of Hezekiah's sons, whom he will father, will be taken away. They will become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

l: Babylonian exile prophecy, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 39
s: Isaiah announces the LORD's word that days are coming when all in Hezekiah's house will be carried to Babylon, and his sons will be taken to serve as eunuchs in the king of Babylon's palace. Hezekiah accepts the word as good, noting that peace and truth will last in his own days.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: Chapter 40 opens with God commanding that his people, and Jerusalem in particular, be comforted because her warfare is over and her iniquity pardoned. A voice calls for the way of the LORD to be prepared in the wilderness, so that his glory is revealed to all flesh, and human frailty is contrasted with the word of God, which stands forever. Messengers to Zion and the cities of Judah are told to announce 'Behold, your God!', who comes with might yet shepherds his flock gently. The text then exalts the LORD as the incomparable Creator, before whom the nations are like a drop in a bucket and the idol made by a workman is no likeness of him. Finally, Jacob and Israel are rebuked for saying their way is hidden from the LORD, and are told that the unwearying God gives strength to the weak and renews those who wait for him.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: The LORD commands that his people be comforted and that a way be prepared for him, and he is announced as coming with a mighty arm while also feeding his flock like a shepherd. He is shown as the incomparable Creator who measures the waters, brings out the stars by name, reduces princes to nothing, never grows weary, and gives power to the weak.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: Jerusalem is to be spoken to comfortably and told that her warfare is accomplished, her iniquity is pardoned, and she has received double from the LORD's hand for all her sins. Along with Zion, she is addressed by messengers who are to lift up their voices and announce 'Behold, your God!'

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: Jacob, together with Israel, is rebuked for complaining that his way is hidden from the LORD and that the justice due him is disregarded by God. He is reminded that the everlasting Creator neither faints nor tires and that his understanding is unsearchable.

l: the nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: The nations are described as a drop in a bucket and a speck of dust on a balance, and as nothing, even less than nothing, before the LORD. Their princes and judges are brought to nothing, withering when he merely blows on them.

l: idol (image cast by workman), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: The idol is described as an image cast by a workman, overlaid with gold by a goldsmith and fitted with silver chains. The poor choose a tree that will not rot and have a skillful workman set up a carved image that will not be moved. It is presented as no answer to the question of whom God can be likened to.

l: grass (metaphor for human frailty), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: All flesh is likened to grass, and its glory to the flower of the field, which withers and fades when the LORD's breath blows on it. The people are said to be like grass, in contrast to the word of God, which stands forever.

l: those who wait for the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 40
s: Those who wait for the LORD are promised renewed strength, in contrast to youths and young men who faint, tire, and fall. They will mount up with wings like eagles, run without weariness, and walk without fainting.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: In Isaiah 41, the LORD summons the islands and peoples to a judgment and asks who raised up one from the east to subdue nations; he answers that he is the first and the last. The nations respond with fear and busy themselves making idols, while the LORD reassures Israel, his servant Jacob, the offspring of Abraham his friend, that he will help and uphold them and make them a threshing instrument against their enemies. He promises to answer the poor and needy by turning the wilderness into pools, springs and groves of trees so that all will know his hand did it. Finally, the LORD challenges the idols to declare the former and coming things, concludes that they and their works are nothing, and says he has raised up one from the north and will send good news to Zion and Jerusalem.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: The LORD summons the nations to judgment, claims to have raised up one from the east and the north, and declares himself the first and with the last. He reassures Israel with promises to help, strengthen and uphold them, calls himself their Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, and promises to answer the poor and needy. He challenges the idols to declare things to come, finds them nothing, and promises to give Jerusalem one who brings good news.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: Israel, called Jacob, the LORD's chosen servant and offspring of Abraham his friend, is told not to fear because the LORD is with them and holds their right hand. Though called a worm, they will be made a new sharp threshing instrument that threshes mountains and hills, and they will rejoice and glory in the Holy One of Israel.

l: one from the east (raised up by the LORD), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: The LORD asks who raised up this one from the east and called him in righteousness, and says he hands nations and kings over to him. His sword and bow make them like dust and driven stubble, and he pursues them and passes on safely by a way he had not gone. Later the LORD says he raised up one from the north, from the rising of the sun, who calls on his name and treads rulers like mortar or clay.

l: islands and peoples, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: The islands and peoples are told to keep silent, renew their strength and come near for judgment. When they see what the LORD has done, they fear, the ends of the earth tremble, and they approach. They encourage one another, as the carpenter, goldsmith and smith strengthen each other in making an idol firm with nails.

l: enemies of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: Those incensed against and striving with Israel are said to be disappointed, confounded, and like nothing, and they will perish. Israel will look for them and not find them, since those who war against Israel will be as a nonexistent thing.

l: idols and false gods, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: The LORD challenges the idols to produce their cause, declare former things and things to come, and do good or evil so that they can be recognized as gods. He pronounces them and their work nothing, and whoever chooses them an abomination. No one among them declares, shows, hears or answers, and their molten images are wind and confusion.

l: waters and streams (in the wilderness), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: The LORD promises to open rivers on the bare heights and springs in the valleys, and to make the wilderness a pool of water and dry land springs, in answer to the poor and needy who seek water. He will plant cedar, acacia, myrtle, oil trees, cypress, pine and box in the desert, so that all may see and understand that the LORD's hand has done this and the Holy One of Israel created it.

l: judgment of the nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 41
s: The LORD calls the islands and peoples to meet together for judgment and opens it with the question of who has raised up the one from the east and worked from the beginning. In the trial he demands that the idols present their strong reasons and predictions, and he concludes that they are nothing, with no counselor who can answer a word.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 42
s: Chapter 42 opens with the LORD presenting his chosen servant, on whom he has put his Spirit, to bring justice to the nations gently and without failing. The LORD, creator of the heavens and earth, calls the servant in righteousness to be a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners. The LORD declares that he will not share his glory with engraved images and announces new things, prompting a call for all the earth, the sea, the islands, the wilderness, Kedar and Sela to sing him a new song. The LORD then says he will break his long silence like a man of war and a travailing woman, lead the blind on unknown paths, and turn back those who trust in idols. The chapter ends by rebuking blind and deaf Israel, a plundered and imprisoned people whom the LORD gave to robbers because they disobeyed his law, and on whom he poured his anger without their taking it to heart.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 42
s: The LORD presents his chosen servant, puts his Spirit on him, and calls him in righteousness to be a covenant for the people and a light for the nations. He is identified as creator of the heavens and earth and giver of breath, who will not give his glory to engraved images, declares new things before they happen, and will go out like a man of war after long silence. He promises to lead the blind on unknown paths and not forsake them, and it is said that he gave Jacob and Israel as plunder because they sinned against him and disobeyed his law.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 42
s: The servant is upheld and chosen by the LORD, who delights in him and puts his Spirit on him. He will bring justice faithfully and gently, not shouting, not breaking a bruised reed or quenching a dimly burning wick, and he will not fail or be discouraged until justice is set on the earth. He is called to be a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners, though a later passage speaks of the LORD's servant and messenger as blind and deaf, seeing many things without observing and having open ears without listening.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 42
s: Jacob, paired with Israel, is described as having been given as plunder to robbers by the LORD. The text says this happened because the people sinned against the LORD, would not walk in his ways, and disobeyed his law.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 42
s: Justice is what the LORD's servant will bring to the nations, faithfully and without being discouraged, until he has set it on the earth. The islands wait for his law. The LORD's own righteousness is also cited as the reason he magnified the law and made it honorable.

l: Israel's punishment, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 42
s: Israel is described as a robbed and plundered people, snared in holes, hidden in prisons, and made captives with no one to deliver them or say 'Restore them!' The LORD gave Jacob and Israel to the robbers because they would not walk in his ways and disobeyed his law. He poured the fierceness of his anger and the strength of battle on him, which set him on fire all around, yet he did not know or take it to heart.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 43
s: In Chapter 43 the LORD tells Jacob and Israel not to fear, because he created and redeemed them, will be with them through water and fire, and will gather their sons and daughters from east, west, north, and south. He calls them his witnesses and declares that he alone is God and Savior, that no one can deliver from his hand, and that he will bring down Babylon and the Chaldeans for their sake. He then tells them to forget former things because he will do a new thing, making a way and rivers in the wilderness so his chosen people may declare his praise. He rebukes Jacob and Israel for not calling on him, for neglecting offerings, and for burdening him with sins, yet says he blots out transgressions for his own sake. The chapter ends with an invitation to plead their case, a charge that their first father and teachers sinned, and a pronouncement that Jacob will become a curse and Israel an insult.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 43
s: The LORD, Creator and Redeemer of Jacob and Israel, promises to be with them through water and fire and declares himself the Holy One, King, and only Savior, with no god before or after him. He vows to gather his scattered people, bring down Babylon and the Chaldeans, do a new thing in the wilderness, and blot out transgressions for his own sake, while also charging Israel with weariness toward him and pronouncing judgment on the sanctuary princes, Jacob, and Israel.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 43
s: Jacob, also called Israel, is told by the LORD not to be afraid, since he is created, redeemed, called by name, and precious and honored in the LORD's sight. He is also accused of not calling on the LORD, of neglecting offerings, and of wearying him with sins, and is finally warned that he will be made a curse.

l: new thing (the LORD's new act in the wilderness), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 43
s: The LORD tells his people to stop remembering former things because he is about to do a new thing that is already springing forth. He will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, giving water to his chosen people so that even jackals and ostriches honor him, and so that the people he formed will declare his praise.

l: sins of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 43
s: The LORD says Israel has not called on him, has been weary of him, and has not brought sheep, sacrifices, or sweet cane, but has burdened and wearied him with sins and iniquities. He nevertheless declares that he blots out their transgressions for his own sake and will not remember them, while noting that their first father sinned and their teachers transgressed, leading to judgment.

l: Israel's dispersed children (sons and daughters), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 43
s: The LORD promises to bring Israel's offspring from the east and gather them from the west, telling the north to give them up and the south not to hold them back. He calls them his sons and daughters from far away and the ends of the earth, everyone called by his name and created, formed, and made for his glory.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: The LORD addresses Jacob, also called Israel and Jeshurun, as his chosen servant, promising to pour out water, his Spirit, and blessing on his descendants. He declares himself the first and the last, with no other God or Rock, and calls Israel his witnesses. The chapter then mocks idol makers, especially the blacksmith and carpenter, who burn part of a tree for warmth and food and then bow to the rest as a god. The LORD assures Israel that he has blotted out its transgressions and redeemed it, and creation is called to sing. He closes by declaring himself creator who frustrates diviners, promises that Jerusalem and Judah's cities will be rebuilt, and names Cyrus as his shepherd who will carry out his pleasure.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: The LORD tells Jacob not to fear, promises to pour water, his Spirit, and blessing on his descendants, and declares himself the first and last with no other God or Rock. He mocks idols, forgives Israel's sins, and identifies himself as Redeemer and maker of all things who stretches out the heavens and spreads out the earth. He frustrates diviners, confirms his servant's word, and names Cyrus as his shepherd.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: Jacob is addressed as the LORD's servant, chosen and formed from the womb, and told not to be afraid. His descendants are promised the outpouring of the Spirit and blessing, and some will take the name of Jacob. He is told to remember that he is the LORD's servant and is redeemed, and the LORD will be glorified in Israel.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: Israel, also called Jeshurun, is chosen by the LORD and called his witnesses to the fact that there is no other God. The LORD says Israel will not be forgotten, that its transgressions are blotted out like a cloud, and that it is redeemed and should return to him. Heaven and earth are called to sing because the LORD will glorify himself in Israel.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: Cyrus is named by the LORD as his shepherd who shall perform all his pleasure. His role is connected to the LORD's word that Jerusalem will be built and the temple's foundation laid.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: The LORD says of Jerusalem that she will be inhabited and built, and that the cities of Judah will be built and their waste places raised up. He also says that the temple's foundation will be laid.

l: idol makers, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: Idol makers are declared vain; their delights do not profit, and their witnesses neither see nor know. The LORD says they and their fellows will be disappointed and put to shame, since the workmen are mere men. Their eyes and hearts are shut so they cannot understand, and one feeds on ashes and is unable to say there is a lie in his right hand.

l: idolatry, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: Idolatry is portrayed as futile and absurd: a man burns part of a tree for warmth and cooking and makes the rest into a god, bowing to it and asking it to deliver him. The text calls this an abomination of a deceived heart and contrasts it with the LORD, who alone is God and Rock.

l: carpenter, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 44
s: The carpenter measures with a line, marks with a pencil, shapes with planes and compasses, and forms wood into the figure of a man to reside in a house. The wood comes from a tree that rain nourished, and part of it is burned for fuel while the rest is made into a god, which the text uses to show the folly of idol making.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 45
s: In Chapter 45, the LORD addresses Cyrus, his anointed, promising to go before him, break open doors of bronze and bars of iron, and give him hidden treasures so that he will know the LORD calls him by name, for the sake of Jacob and Israel. The LORD declares that there is no other God, that he forms light and darkness and makes peace and calamity, and warns that no one may strive with their Maker. He says Cyrus will rebuild his city and free his exiles without price or reward, and that Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Sabeans will come over to Cyrus in chains confessing that God is with him. Idol makers will be confounded, while Israel will be saved with an everlasting salvation. The LORD calls all the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved, swearing that every knee will bow to him and that all Israel's offspring will be justified and rejoice.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 45
s: The LORD calls Cyrus his anointed, promises to go before him and open doors, and declares himself the only God, creator of light and darkness, peace and calamity, heavens and earth. He rebukes those who strive with their Maker, says he has not spoken in secret, and swears that every knee will bow to him and that all the ends of the earth should look to him and be saved.

l: Cyrus, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 45
s: Cyrus is addressed as the LORD's anointed, whose right hand the LORD has held to subdue nations and strip kings of their armor. The LORD promises him treasures of darkness and hidden riches, names him though he has not known the LORD, and says he will build the LORD's city and free the exiles without price or reward. Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Sabeans are to come over to him in chains and acknowledge that God is in him.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 45
s: Israel, called the LORD's chosen, and Jacob his servant, are the reason the LORD has called Cyrus by name. The chapter promises that Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation and never be disappointed or confounded. All of Israel's offspring will be justified in the LORD and will rejoice.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: Chapter 46 contrasts the helpless idols of Bel and Nebo with God, who carries his people. Bel and Nebo bow down, and their idols are loaded onto animals as a burden, going into captivity because they cannot deliver it. God then addresses the house of Jacob and the remnant of the house of Israel, saying he has carried them from birth to old age and will deliver them. God asks to whom he can be compared, mocking those who pay a goldsmith to make a god that must be carried, cannot move, and cannot answer or save. He declares that he is God, that there is no other, that he declares the end from the beginning, and that his counsel will stand. He calls a ravenous bird from the east to carry out his plan, tells the stubborn-hearted that his righteousness and salvation are near, and promises salvation to Zion and glory to Israel.

l: Bel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: Bel bows down together with Nebo as the text opens. Bel is shown as helpless, since its idols are loaded onto animals and cannot deliver their burden but go into captivity.

l: Nebo, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: Nebo stoops and bows down together with Bel. Its idols are carried by animals as heavy loads, are unable to deliver the burden, and go into captivity.

l: idols (of Bel and Nebo), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: The idols are carried on animals and livestock as heavy loads, a burden for the weary. They cannot deliver the burden, and they themselves go into captivity.

l: house of Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: The house of Jacob is called by God to listen. It is told that it has been carried by him from birth and from the womb, and that he will carry and deliver it even to old age and gray hairs.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: The remnant of the house of Israel is addressed alongside the house of Jacob as those God has carried from birth. God promises to grant his glory to Israel and salvation to Zion.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: God declares that he carries and delivers his people, that there is no other God and none like him, and that he declares the end from the beginning. He says his counsel will stand, that he calls a ravenous bird from the east to fulfill his plan, and that his righteousness and salvation are near and will not wait.

l: god (made by goldsmith), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 46
s: This god is made by a goldsmith hired by people who pour out gold and weigh silver. It is carried on shoulders and set in its place, where it stays unable to move, cannot answer those who cry to it, and cannot save anyone from trouble.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 47
s: Chapter 47 is a pronouncement against the virgin daughter of Babylon, the daughter of the Chaldeans, who is ordered down from her throne to sit in the dust, do menial work, and suffer public shame. The LORD of Armies, called Redeemer and Holy One of Israel, declares that he will take vengeance and spare no one. He says he gave his angry people into her hand, but she showed no mercy and laid a heavy yoke on the aged. She is condemned for her pride, her pleasure-seeking security, her claim 'I am, and there is no one else besides me,' and her trust in wickedness, sorceries, and enchantments. Sudden disaster, loss of children and widowhood will come on her in one day, and her astrologers and former trading partners will be unable to save her.

l: daughter of Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 47
s: The virgin daughter of Babylon, also called the daughter of the Chaldeans, is told to come down from her throne and sit in the dust and in silence and darkness. She will grind flour, be stripped of her veil, and have her nakedness and shame exposed, and she will no longer be called tender, delicate, or mistress of kingdoms. She showed Israel no mercy, laid a heavy yoke on the aged, said she would be a princess forever, and boasted 'I am, and there is no one else besides me.' Widowhood and loss of children will come on her in one day, and no one will save her.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 47
s: The LORD of Armies, named as Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel, speaks vengeance against Babylon and says he will spare no one. He reveals that he was angry with his people, profaned his inheritance, and gave them into Babylon's hand. He is the one who brings the coming disaster on her.

l: astrologers and prognosticators, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 47
s: The astrologers, stargazers, and monthly prognosticators are challenged to stand up and save Babylon from what will happen to her. They are described as like stubble that fire will burn, unable to deliver even themselves from the flame. Their fire will give no warmth, and they offer no rescue.

l: sorceries and enchantments (Babylon's), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 47
s: Babylon's sorceries and enchantments are things she has labored in since her youth, hoping to profit and prevail. They are present in great multitude and abundance, yet the widowhood and loss of children will come on her in full measure despite them. She is told to stand with them, but they cannot save her, and her wisdom and knowledge are said to have perverted her.

l: disaster (coming on Babylon), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 47
s: Disaster, mischief, and desolation are announced as coming on Babylon suddenly, in a way she will not know when it dawns, cannot put away, and does not understand. It includes the loss of children and widowhood arriving in a moment in one day. It comes because she trusted in her wickedness and said 'No one sees me.'

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 48
s: The LORD addresses the house of Jacob, who swear by his name but not in truth, and reminds them that he declared former things long ago so they could not credit an idol. He now announces new, hidden things and says he withholds his anger for his own name's sake, having refined them in the furnace of affliction. He declares himself the first and the last and the creator of earth and heavens, and says that the one he loves will act against Babylon and the Chaldeans. He laments that Israel did not heed his commandments, which would have brought peace like a river, and then calls them to leave Babylon and proclaim that he has redeemed his servant Jacob. The chapter closes with the reminder of water from the rock in the deserts and the statement that there is no peace for the wicked.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 48
s: The LORD rebukes the house of Jacob for insincere oaths and declares that he announced former things beforehand because he knew their obstinacy. He defers his anger for his name's sake, refines them in affliction, and affirms he is the first and the last, who founded the earth and spread the heavens. He teaches and leads his people, laments their disobedience, and redeems his servant Jacob, declaring there is no peace for the wicked.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 48
s: Jacob, also called Israel and the house of Jacob, is accused of swearing by the LORD's name without truth or righteousness and of being obstinate, treacherous, and a transgressor from the womb. The LORD spares and refines him in the furnace of affliction, and says that obedience would have brought peace like a river and offspring like sand. Jacob is called to leave Babylon, and it is proclaimed that the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob.

l: Babylon, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 48
s: Babylon, along with the Chaldeans, is named as the target of the one whom the LORD loves, who will do what he likes to it, with his arm against the Chaldeans. The people are told to leave Babylon and flee from the Chaldeans.

l: one from the east (raised up by the LORD), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 48
s: He whom the LORD loves is said to do what he likes to Babylon, with his arm against the Chaldeans. The LORD says he has spoken, called him, and brought him, and that this man will make his way prosperous.

l: former and new things (the LORD's declared acts), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 48
s: The former things were declared by the LORD long ago, then done suddenly and fulfilled, so that Israel could not attribute them to an idol or image. The new things are hidden, created now and not from of old, and were not heard before today so that Israel could not claim to have known them already.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: In Isaiah 49, a speaker called by the LORD from the womb and named his servant, Israel, says he has labored in vain but trusts the LORD for his reward. The LORD answers that restoring Jacob's tribes is too light a task and makes him a light to the nations and a covenant for the people, so that kings will rise and worship. The LORD promises to free the bound, lead them to pasture and springs, and gather them from afar, and the heavens and earth are called to sing. Zion says the LORD has forsaken her, but he replies that he will not forget her, since he has engraved her on his palms, and he promises her children will return and crowd her. The LORD will lift his banner to the nations so they carry her sons and daughters, and he will rescue the captives of the mighty and judge her oppressors so that all flesh knows he is Savior and Redeemer.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: The LORD called his servant from the womb, assigns him to restore Jacob and be a light to the nations, and promises to free the bound and lead them by springs of water. He declares he will not forget Zion, having engraved her on his palms, and will contend with her oppressors and save her children. His acts will make all flesh know he is Savior, Redeemer, and the Mighty One of Jacob.

l: Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: The servant says the LORD called him from the womb, made his mouth like a sharp sword, and hid him in his quiver. He laments having labored in vain but trusts the LORD for justice and reward. The LORD tells him that raising up Jacob is too light a task and gives him as a light to the nations and a covenant for the people, though he is despised by man and abhorred by the nation, and kings will rise and worship.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: Israel is named as the LORD's servant in whom he will be glorified, and the LORD speaks of bringing Jacob back to him and gathering Israel. The LORD is called the Redeemer of Israel, and the Holy One of Israel is said to have chosen the servant.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: Zion complains that the LORD has forsaken and forgotten her. The LORD answers that even if a mother might forget her child, he will not forget her, and her walls are always before him. She is promised that her land will become too small for her returning inhabitants, that she will wear them like a bride's ornament, and that her devourers will be far away.

l: sons of Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: Zion's children hurry back while her destroyers leave, and they gather from all around to come to her. Born in her bereavement, they say the place is too small and ask for room to live. The nations will carry her sons in their bosoms and her daughters on their shoulders, and the LORD will save them from those who contend with her.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 49
s: The LORD will make his servant a light to the nations, and he will lift his hand and banner to them. They will bring Zion's sons and daughters, and their kings and queens will act as foster fathers and nursing mothers, bowing to her with their faces to the earth. Kings also see and rise up, and princes worship, because of the faithful LORD.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 50
s: In Chapter 50, the LORD challenges the people by asking where the divorce certificate for their mother is and to which creditor he sold them, declaring that they were sold for their iniquities and their mother put away for their transgressions. He asks why no one answered when he came and called, insisting that his hand is not shortened and that he can redeem, as shown by his power to dry up the sea and clothe the heavens with blackness. A speaker, the servant of the Lord GOD, then describes being given the tongue of the taught to sustain the weary, and having his ear opened so that he was not rebellious. He tells of giving his back to those who beat him and not hiding his face from shame and spitting, trusting that the Lord GOD will help him and that his adversaries will wear out like a moth-eaten garment. The chapter closes with a call for those who fear the LORD to trust his name while walking in darkness, and a warning that those who kindle their own fires will lie down in sorrow.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 50
s: The LORD asks where the bill of divorce is and which creditor he sold the people to, stating that they were sold for their iniquities and their mother put away for their transgressions. He asks why no one answered when he came and called, affirms that his hand is not shortened and that he has power to redeem and deliver, and points to his rebuke that dries up the sea and his clothing of the heavens with blackness.

l: the speaker (the Lord GOD's servant), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 50
s: The speaker says the Lord GOD gave him the tongue of the taught to sustain the weary with words, and opened his ear morning by morning so that he was not rebellious and did not turn back. He gave his back to those who beat him and his cheeks to those who plucked out the hair, and did not hide from shame and spitting. He sets his face like flint, trusts that the Lord GOD will help him, and challenges any adversary or accuser to come near, since the one who justifies him is near.

l: mother (of the addressed people), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 50
s: The mother is said to have been put away because of the transgressions of her children. The LORD asks where the bill of her divorce is, implying that no such document exists to show he cast her off permanently.

l: the addressed people (children of the mother), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 50
s: The addressed people are told they were sold for their iniquities, and the LORD asks to which of his creditors he sold them. They are rebuked because no one was there or answered when he came and called. The servant's voice is to be obeyed by those who fear the LORD, and those walking in darkness are urged to trust the LORD's name, while those who kindle their own fires and torches are warned they will lie down in sorrow.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: In Isaiah 51, the LORD calls on those who pursue righteousness to remember Abraham and Sarah, and promises to comfort Zion and turn her wastes into Eden. He declares that his righteousness and salvation are near and will last forever, though the heavens and earth will wear out, so his people should not fear the insults of men. A voice then calls on the arm of the LORD to awake as in the days when he cut Rahab in pieces and dried up the sea, and the ransomed are promised a joyful return to Zion. The LORD rebukes the fear of mortal men and the oppressor, and promises the captive exile freedom. He then addresses Jerusalem, which has drunk the cup of his wrath and has no one to guide her, and announces that he has taken the cup from her hand and will put it into the hands of her oppressors.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: The LORD calls his people to listen, promises to comfort Zion, and says his righteousness and salvation are near and will last forever. He is called upon to awake as the one who cut Rahab in pieces and dried up the sea, and he identifies himself as the Maker who stretched out the heavens and stirs up the sea. He takes the cup of wrath from Jerusalem and puts it into the hands of her oppressors.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: Zion is comforted by the LORD, who makes her waste places and wilderness like Eden and the garden of the LORD, filled with joy, gladness, thanksgiving, and melody. The ransomed will return to her with singing, and the LORD will tell her, 'You are my people.'

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: Jerusalem is told to awake and stand up, having drunk and drained the cup of the LORD's wrath and staggered. She has no one to guide her, her sons lie fainted at the head of the streets like an antelope in a net, and she suffers desolation, destruction, famine, and the sword. The LORD then declares he has taken the cup from her hand and she will not drink it any more.

l: righteous followers (those who seek the LORD), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: Those who follow after righteousness and seek the LORD are told to look to the rock they were cut from and to Abraham and Sarah. Those who know righteousness and have his law in their hearts are told not to fear the reproach or insults of men, who will be eaten like a garment by the moth.

l: The Holy People, The LORD’s Redeemed, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: The redeemed are recalled as those for whom the LORD made the depths of the sea a way to pass over. The ransomed will return and come with singing to Zion, with everlasting joy on their heads, while sorrow and sighing flee away.

l: cup of the LORD's wrath, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: Jerusalem has drunk the cup of staggering, the bowl of the LORD's wrath, and drained it, leaving her sons full of the LORD's wrath. The LORD declares he has taken it out of her hand so she will not drink it any more, and will put it into the hand of those who afflict her.

l: righteousness and salvation, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 51
s: The LORD says his righteousness is near and his salvation has gone out, and his justice will be a light to the peoples. Though the heavens vanish like smoke and the earth wears out like a garment, his salvation will be forever and his righteousness will not be abolished, lasting to all generations.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: Chapter 52 summons Zion and Jerusalem to awake, put on strength and beautiful garments, and shake off the dust and bonds of captivity, since the unclean will no longer enter the holy city. The LORD declares that his people, who went down into Egypt and were oppressed by the Assyrian, were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money, so that they will know his name. A herald on the mountains brings good news of peace and salvation, proclaiming 'Your God reigns,' and the watchmen and the waste places of Jerusalem sing because the LORD has comforted and redeemed his people and bared his holy arm before all nations. The people are told to depart, cleanse themselves, and leave without haste, with the LORD going before them and as their rear guard. The chapter closes with the LORD's servant, who will deal wisely and be exalted, whose appearance was marred and who will cleanse many nations while kings shut their mouths in astonishment.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: Zion is urged to awake and put on her strength, and the captive daughter of Zion is told to release herself from the bonds of her neck. Someone proclaims to Zion, 'Your God reigns,' and the LORD is said to be returning to her.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: Jerusalem, called the holy city, is told to put on beautiful garments, shake off the dust, and sit up, because the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter it. Its waste places are called to sing together because the LORD has comforted his people and redeemed Jerusalem.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: The LORD declares that his people were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money, and that his name is blasphemed continually while they are taken away. He will make his holy arm bare before all nations, return to Zion, and go before his people as well as guard their rear, so that they will know he is the one who speaks.

l: my people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: The LORD's people went down into Egypt to live, were oppressed without cause by the Assyrian, and are now taken away for nothing and mocked by their rulers. They are promised redemption without money, will come to know the LORD's name, and are told to depart, touch nothing unclean, and cleanse themselves, going out neither in haste nor in flight.

l: him who brings good news, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: He is described as beautiful on the mountains by his feet, as one who publishes peace and proclaims salvation. He says to Zion, 'Your God reigns!'

l: my servant, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: The LORD's servant will deal wisely and be exalted, lifted up, and very high. Many were astonished at him because his appearance and form were marred more than any man's, and he will cleanse many nations while kings shut their mouths at him, seeing and understanding what they had not been told or heard.

l: redemption, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 52
s: The LORD says his people, sold for nothing, will be redeemed without money. The text states that the LORD has comforted his people and redeemed Jerusalem, and that all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 53
s: Chapter 53 describes a servant who grew up like a tender plant, was unattractive, despised and rejected, and acquainted with suffering and disease. The speakers ("we") confess that they wrongly thought God had struck him, when in fact he was pierced and crushed for their transgressions and iniquities, bringing them peace and healing. The LORD laid the iniquity of all on him; he was oppressed and silent like a lamb led to slaughter, cut off from the land of the living, and given a grave with the wicked and a rich man despite his innocence. It pleased the LORD to bruise him and make his soul an offering for sin, after which he will see his offspring, prolong his days, see the light, and be satisfied. The LORD promises him a portion with the great and the strong, because he poured out his soul to death, was counted with transgressors, bore the sins of many, and interceded for them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 53
s: The LORD's arm is asked about as something revealed to few, and he is said to have laid the iniquity of all on his servant. It pleased him to bruise the servant and make his soul an offering for sin, and he promises the servant a portion with the great and the strong, with his pleasure prospering in the servant's hand.

l: the suffering servant (he), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 53
s: The servant grew up as a tender plant and a root out of dry ground, without beauty or majesty, and was despised, rejected, and acquainted with suffering. He was pierced, crushed, oppressed, and silent like a lamb, was cut off, and was buried with the wicked and a rich man though he had done no violence and spoken no deceit. He will see offspring, prolong his days, see the light and be satisfied, justify many, bear their iniquities, and receive a portion with the great as one who interceded for transgressors.

l: we (the speakers), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 53
s: The speakers ask who has believed their message, admit they did not desire or respect the servant, and confess they considered him plagued and struck by God. They come to see that he bore their sickness and was pierced for their transgressions, and that they, like sheep, had all gone astray, each turning to his own way. Through his punishment and wounds they receive peace and healing.

l: the servant's suffering and death, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 53
s: The servant's suffering is described as bearing sickness and sorrow, being pierced, crushed, bruised, oppressed, and taken away to death, where he was cut off from the land of the living. It is borne for the transgressions and iniquities of others and brings them peace and healing. It is made an offering for sin and is followed by the servant seeing light, being satisfied, and receiving a portion with the great.

l: iniquity and sin, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 53
s: The speakers' transgressions and iniquities are the reason the servant was pierced and crushed, and all have gone astray, each to his own way. The LORD laid the iniquity of all on the servant, who bears the iniquities and sins of many, justifies many, and intercedes for the transgressors.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 54
s: Chapter 54 is the LORD's address to a barren, desolate woman, a figure for Israel, urging her to sing and enlarge her tent because her children will outnumber those of the married wife and will possess the nations. The LORD promises she will forget the shame of her youth and widowhood, since her Maker is her husband and the Holy One of Israel is her Redeemer. He admits forsaking her for a moment in overflowing wrath, but vows everlasting loving kindness, comparing his oath to the waters of Noah. He says the mountains may depart before his loving kindness and covenant of peace do. He promises to rebuild the afflicted city with sapphires, rubies, and precious stones, to have her children taught by himself, and to establish her in righteousness. No weapon formed against her will prevail, and this is declared the heritage of the LORD's servants.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 54
s: The LORD addresses the barren, desolate woman, calling her to sing and enlarge her tent. He identifies himself as her Maker, husband, and Redeemer, the LORD of Armies and God of the whole earth. He admits he forsook her for a moment in wrath but will gather her with great mercies and everlasting loving kindness, swearing as he did after the waters of Noah not to be angry with her again. He promises to rebuild her with jewels, teach her children, and establish her in righteousness. He says he created both the blacksmith and the destroyer, that gatherings against her are not from him, and that no weapon formed against her will prevail.

l: Israel, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 54
s: Israel is addressed under the figure of a barren, desolate, forsaken wife and widow, and the LORD is called the Holy One of Israel, her Redeemer. Though cast off for a moment, she is promised restoration, an enlarged dwelling, a city adorned with precious stones, freedom from shame, oppression, and terror, and victory over every accusing tongue.

l: children of Israel (the barren woman's children), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 54
s: The woman's children are said to be more numerous than those of the married wife. They will spread right and left, possess the nations, and settle desolate cities. All of them will be taught by the LORD, and their peace will be great.

l: covenant of peace, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 54
s: The LORD calls his covenant of peace unremovable: the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but it will not be removed from the afflicted woman. It is tied to his sworn promise, likened to the waters of Noah, not to be angry with her or rebuke her.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 55
s: In Chapter 55 the LORD invites everyone who thirsts to come to the waters and receive food, wine, and milk without money or price, asking why they spend labor on what does not satisfy. He promises an everlasting covenant, the sure mercies of David, and says he has given a witness, leader, and commander to the peoples; a nation unknown to the addressee will run to it because the LORD has glorified it. The people are urged to seek the LORD while he is near, and the wicked man is told to forsake his way and thoughts and return, for the LORD will freely pardon. The LORD declares that his thoughts and ways are higher than human ones as the heavens are higher than the earth, and that his word, like rain and snow that water the earth, will not return void but will accomplish what he pleases. The chapter ends with a promise of going out with joy and peace, singing mountains and clapping trees, and cypress and myrtle replacing thorn and brier as an everlasting sign making a name for the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 55
s: The LORD invites all who thirst to come and receive food and drink freely, and promises an everlasting covenant, the sure mercies of David. He urges people to seek him while he is near and promises mercy and free pardon to those who return. He declares that his thoughts and ways are higher than human ones, and that he will glorify his people and make a name for himself through an everlasting sign.

l: everyone who thirsts (addressees of the invitation), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 55
s: They are called to come to the waters and to buy and eat without money and without price. They are asked why they spend money and labor on what does not satisfy, and are told to listen, turn their ear, and come so that their souls will live. They are promised that they will go out with joy and peace, and that nature will sing and clap for them.

l: everlasting covenant (with David), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 55
s: The LORD promises to make an everlasting covenant with the listeners, described as the sure mercies of David. In connection with it, he says he has given a witness, a leader and commander, to the peoples, and that nations will run to the one he has glorified.

l: wicked man (who should repent), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 55
s: The wicked man is told to forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and to return to the LORD. If he does, the LORD will have mercy on him and freely pardon.

l: word of the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 55
s: The LORD's word is compared to rain and snow that come down, water the earth, make it grow and give seed and bread, and do not return empty. It will not return void but will accomplish what the LORD pleases and prosper in the thing it was sent to do.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: In Chapter 56 the LORD calls his people to maintain justice and do what is right, because his salvation is near and his righteousness will soon be revealed.
