He blesses those who keep the Sabbath without profaning it and keep their hands from evil. He assures foreigners who join themselves to him and eunuchs who keep his Sabbaths and hold fast his covenant that they will not be separated from his people: eunuchs will receive an everlasting name better than sons and daughters, and foreigners will be brought to his holy mountain, where their offerings will be accepted in his house, called a house of prayer for all peoples. The Lord GOD, who gathers Israel's outcasts, promises to gather still others in addition to those already gathered. The chapter ends by summoning the animals of the field and forest to devour, and condemns Israel's watchmen as blind, ignorant, mute dogs who are greedy, lack understanding, pursue their own gain, and plan to indulge in wine and strong drink, expecting tomorrow to be like today.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: The LORD commands his people to maintain justice and do what is right, declaring that his salvation is near and his righteousness will soon be revealed. He promises eunuchs an everlasting name and foreigners a place on his holy mountain and in his house of prayer, and, as the Lord GOD who gathers Israel's outcasts, says he will gather others in addition to those already gathered.

l: foreigners (who join the LORD), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: Foreigners who join themselves to the LORD are told not to say that he will surely separate them from his people. If they serve him, love his name, keep the Sabbath without profaning it, and hold fast his covenant, he will bring them to his holy mountain, make them joyful in his house of prayer, and accept their burnt offerings and sacrifices on his altar.

l: eunuchs, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: Eunuchs are told not to say, "Behold, I am a dry tree." To those who keep the LORD's Sabbaths, choose what pleases him, and hold fast his covenant, he promises a memorial and a name within his house and walls, better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that will not be cut off.

l: Sabbath, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: Keeping the Sabbath without profaning it is named as a mark of the blessed person and is paired with keeping one's hand from evil. Both eunuchs and foreigners who keep it and hold fast the LORD's covenant receive his promises.

l: house of prayer (the LORD's house), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: The LORD promises to make foreigners joyful in his house of prayer, where their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on his altar. He declares that his house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: The LORD commands his people to maintain justice and do what is right, giving as the reason that his salvation is near and his righteousness will soon be revealed. Holding fast to this is described as bringing blessing.

l: watchmen (Israel's blind watchmen), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 56
s: Israel's watchmen are described as blind, without knowledge, and like mute dogs who cannot bark, dreaming, lying down, and loving to slumber. They are also called greedy dogs and shepherds who cannot understand, each turning to his own way and gain, and they plan to fill themselves with wine and strong drink, assuming tomorrow will be as today, great beyond measure.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: Chapter 57 opens by lamenting that the righteous and merciful perish unnoticed, though they enter peace and rest. The LORD then summons the 'sons of a sorceress', offspring of adulterers and prostitutes, and condemns their mockery and their idolatrous practices: burning with passion among oaks, killing children in the valleys, offering drink offerings to smooth stones, setting a bed on high mountains, and seeking alliances with a king and sending ambassadors as far as Sheol. He says their works will not benefit them, that the idols they gathered will be carried off by the wind, while whoever takes refuge in him will inherit the land and his holy mountain. The high and holy One who dwells with the contrite and humble promises to revive them, says he will not contend forever, and declares that he will heal and lead the backsliding one and give peace to those far and near. The chapter closes by comparing the wicked to a troubled sea and stating that there is no peace for them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: The LORD summons and condemns the 'sons of a sorceress' for their idolatry and falsehood, saying he has long held his peace and that their works will not benefit them. He is described as the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, dwelling in the high and holy place and with the contrite and humble. He says he will not contend forever or be always angry, admits he struck and hid from the backsliding one, and promises to heal, lead, and comfort him, creating 'the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace' for those far and near. He declares there is no peace for the wicked.

l: the righteous, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: The righteous and merciful perish and are taken away, and no one lays it to heart or considers that they are taken away from the evil. They enter into peace and rest in their beds, each one who walks in his uprightness.

l: the addressed people (children of the mother), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: Addressed as sons of a sorceress and offspring of adulterers and prostitutes, they are rebuked for mocking, and called children of disobedience and falsehood. They practice idol worship among oaks, kill children in valleys, offer to smooth stones, set their bed on a high mountain, and send ambassadors far off, even degrading themselves to Sheol. Though wearied, they never say 'in vain'. The LORD says he will declare their righteousness, their works will not benefit them, and the wind will carry away the idols they gathered.

l: the wicked, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: The wicked are likened to the troubled sea that cannot rest and casts up mire and mud. The chapter ends with the LORD's declaration, 'There is no peace for the wicked.'

l: the humble and contrite, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: The LORD dwells in the high and holy place with those of a contrite and humble spirit, and promises to revive both their spirit and their heart. Those who take refuge in him will possess the land and inherit his holy mountain, and the way is to be prepared and stumbling-blocks removed for his people.

l: idolatrous worship, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: Idolatrous worship is depicted as including burning with passion among oaks and under green trees, child killing in the valleys, drink and other offerings to smooth stones, and sacrifices on a high mountain. It also includes memorials set behind doors and posts, a bed made into a covenant with others than the LORD, and seeking a king with oil and perfumes. The LORD asks whether he will be appeased by these, and says the gathered idols will be carried away by wind and breath.

l: peace, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: Peace is what the righteous enter and rest in at death. The LORD creates 'Peace, peace' as the fruit of the lips for those far and near. It is denied to the wicked, for whom the LORD says there is none.

l: healing and restoration, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 57
s: The LORD says he has seen the backsliding one's ways and will heal him, lead him, and restore comforts to him and his mourners. He will revive the spirit of the humble and the heart of the contrite, and says again that he will heal those far off and near. His anger is not forever, since the spirit and souls he made would faint before him.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: In Chapter 58 the LORD commands a prophetic voice to cry aloud and declare to his people, the house of Jacob, their disobedience. The people seek God daily and complain that their fasting goes unnoticed, but the LORD answers that they pursue pleasure and oppress their laborers while fasting amid strife and contention. He defines the fast he has chosen as releasing the bonds of wickedness, freeing the oppressed, sharing bread with the hungry, sheltering the poor, and covering the naked. For such obedience he promises light, healing, guidance, strength, restoration, and the name Repairer of the Breach. He also calls them to honor the Sabbath as a delight rather than pursuing their own pleasure, promising delight in the LORD and the heritage of Jacob their father.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The LORD commands that his people's sins be proclaimed loudly and rebukes their fasting as self-serving. He defines the fast he has chosen as justice and mercy, and promises to answer, guide, heal, and satisfy those who obey, saying 'Here I am.' He also calls the Sabbath his holy day and says his mouth has spoken these promises.

l: house of Jacob, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The house of Jacob is charged with disobedience and sins, even though they seek God daily and delight to know his ways. They complain that their fasts go unnoticed, but are told they oppress laborers and fast for strife. They are offered restoration and called to build old waste places, with the promise of being fed with the heritage of Jacob their father.

l: fast (true fast), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The people's fast, with bowed heads, sackcloth, and ashes, is rejected because it coexists with pleasure-seeking, oppression, and strife. The LORD states that the fast he has chosen is to release the bonds of wickedness, undo the yoke, let the oppressed go free, feed the hungry, shelter the poor, and clothe the naked.

l: oppression and injustice, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The people are accused of oppressing all their laborers and fasting for strife, contention, and striking with the fist of wickedness. They are told to remove the yoke, finger pointing, and wicked speech. Ending these is the condition for the LORD's blessing.

l: the oppressed and needy, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The oppressed, hungry, poor cast out, and naked are the ones the people are told to free, feed, house, and cover. The text says the people should not hide themselves from their own flesh. Caring for the afflicted soul is tied directly to the people's own blessing.

l: Sabbath, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The Sabbath is called the LORD's holy day, and the people are told to turn their foot from doing their own pleasure, ways, and words on it. They are to call it a delight and honor it as holy to the LORD. Doing so leads to delighting in the LORD, riding on the high places of the earth, and being fed with the heritage of Jacob.

l: blessings of righteousness, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 58
s: The LORD promises that obedience will bring light breaking out like morning, quick healing, righteousness going before, and his glory as rear guard. He will answer when they call, guide them continually, satisfy them in dry places, strengthen their bones, and make them like a watered garden. They will rebuild old waste places and be called Repairer of the Breach, Restorer of Paths with Dwellings.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: Chapter 59 declares that the LORD's hand is not too short to save nor his ear too dull to hear, but that the people's iniquities have separated them from God. The passage details their bloodshed, lies, and violence, and the people confess that justice and righteousness are far from them and that they grope in darkness. The LORD sees that there is no justice and no intercessor, so his own arm brings salvation, and he puts on righteousness, salvation, vengeance, and zeal as armor and clothing. He will repay adversaries according to their deeds, and people from west to east will fear his name. The chapter ends with the promise that a Redeemer will come to Zion and to those in Jacob who turn from disobedience, and with the LORD's covenant that his Spirit and words will remain with the people and their descendants forever.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: The LORD is declared able to save and hear, though the people's sins have hidden his face from them. He sees there is no justice and no intercessor, so his own arm brings salvation; he puts on righteousness, a helmet of salvation, vengeance, and zeal, and promises to repay adversaries and enemies. He announces a Redeemer for Zion and establishes his covenant of his Spirit and words with the people and their offspring forever.

l: the people (addressed as you/we), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: The people are accused of defiled hands, lying lips, violence, and hurrying to shed innocent blood, and their iniquities have separated them from God. They confess that they grope like the blind, look for justice and salvation that are far off, and know their transgressions, including denying the LORD and speaking falsehood. Those in Jacob who turn from disobedience are promised a Redeemer and the LORD's covenant, with his words remaining in their mouths and those of their descendants.

l: Redeemer, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: A Redeemer is promised by the LORD as one who will come to Zion. He comes to those in Jacob who turn from disobedience.

l: iniquity and sin, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: Iniquities and sins are said to separate the people from God and hide his face so that he will not hear. They are described as bloody hands, lies, conceived mischief, adders' eggs and spider webs that yield no covering, and the people acknowledge that their transgressions testify against them. The LORD's response includes repaying according to deeds, and a Redeemer for those who turn from disobedience.

l: justice, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: Justice is described as absent: the people do not know the way of peace, justice is far from them, turned backward, and truth has fallen in the street. The LORD is displeased to see that there is no justice, and responds by acting himself with his own arm and righteousness.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 59
s: The LORD declares his covenant with the people: his Spirit on them and his words in their mouths will not depart from them, their offspring, or their offspring's offspring. It is to last from now on and forever.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: Chapter 60 addresses Zion, told to arise and shine because the LORD's light and glory have come upon her while darkness covers the earth and peoples. Nations and kings are drawn to her brightness, and her sons and daughters return from far away. Peoples from places such as Midian, Ephah, Sheba, Kedar, Nebaioth, Lebanon, and Tarshish bring gold, frankincense, flocks, ships, silver, and timber to honor the LORD and beautify his house. Foreigners rebuild her walls, former oppressors bow to her, and nations that refuse to serve her perish. The LORD promises to turn her from forsaken to an eternal excellency, to replace violence with peace and righteousness, to be her everlasting light instead of sun and moon, and to make her people righteous and numerous.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: The LORD arises on Zion with his glory, having struck her in wrath but shown mercy in favor. He promises to beautify his house and sanctuary, to make Zion an eternal joy, to be her Savior, Redeemer, and everlasting light, and to multiply her people quickly in its time.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: Zion is commanded to arise and shine, as her light has come and the LORD's glory is on her. Once forsaken and hated, she is promised to become an eternal excellency and a joy of many generations, with open gates, walls called Salvation, gates called Praise, and peace and righteousness as her rulers. She will be called the LORD's City, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel.

l: nations, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: Nations and kings come to Zion's light, bringing their wealth, serving her, and building her walls, while former oppressors bow at her feet. Any nation or kingdom that will not serve her perishes and is utterly wasted.

l: Zion's sons and daughters (Zion), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: Zion's sons come from far away and her daughters are carried in arms as they gather to her. Ships of Tarshish bring the sons along with their silver and gold. In the end, her people are all righteous, inherit the land forever, and the little one becomes a thousand and the small one a strong nation.

l: light and glory, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: Light and glory rise on Zion while thick darkness covers the earth, drawing nations to her brightness. The sun and moon are replaced: the LORD becomes her everlasting light and her God her glory, so her sun never goes down and her mourning ends.

l: wealth and tribute, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 60
s: The abundance of the sea and the wealth of the nations flow to Zion, including camels, gold, frankincense, flocks, rams for the altar, silver, and Lebanon's cypress, pine, and box wood. These are brought through gates that stay open continually, to proclaim the LORD's praises and beautify his sanctuary. The LORD also promises to give gold for bronze, silver for iron, bronze for wood, and iron for stones.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 61
s: In Chapter 61, a speaker whom the Lord GOD's Spirit rests upon and who has been anointed announces good news to the humble, healing for the broken hearted, liberty for captives, and the year of the LORD's favor alongside the day of vengeance. Those who mourn in Zion receive a garland, the oil of joy, and the garment of praise, and are called trees of righteousness. The people will rebuild old ruins, while strangers and foreigners tend their flocks and fields, and they will be called the LORD's priests and servants of God, eating the wealth of the nations and receiving double for their shame. The LORD declares that he loves justice, hates robbery and iniquity, and will make an everlasting covenant, so that their offspring are acknowledged among the nations as blessed. The speaker rejoices, clothed with salvation and righteousness like a bridegroom or bride, and says the Lord GOD will make righteousness and praise spring up before all nations.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 61
s: The Lord GOD's Spirit is on the speaker, and the LORD has anointed him to preach good news and proclaim liberty, favor, and vengeance. He declares that he loves justice, hates robbery and iniquity, will reward his people in truth, and will make an everlasting covenant with them. He is also said to cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.

l: speaker (anointed preacher), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 61
s: The speaker says the LORD has anointed and sent him to preach good news to the humble, bind up the broken hearted, proclaim liberty to captives, and comfort all who mourn. He rejoices greatly in the LORD, saying he has been clothed with the garments of salvation and covered with the robe of righteousness, like a bridegroom or a bride.

l: Zion's people (Zion), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 61
s: The mourners in Zion are to be provided for and comforted. They receive a garland for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. They will be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, so that he may be glorified.

l: the addressed people (Israel, God's priests), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 61
s: The addressed people will rebuild the old ruins and devastated cities, while strangers and foreigners feed their flocks and work their fields and vineyards. They will be called the LORD's priests and servants of our God, eat the wealth of the nations, and possess a double portion with everlasting joy. Their offspring will be known among the nations and acknowledged as blessed by the LORD.

l: righteousness and praise, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 61
s: Righteousness and praise are said to be something the Lord GOD will cause to spring up before all the nations. The comparison is to the earth producing its bud and a garden causing its sown seeds to spring up.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: Chapter 62 has a speaker vowing not to stay silent for the sake of Zion and Jerusalem until her righteousness and salvation shine out. The LORD promises that the nations and kings will see her glory and that she will receive a new name, becoming a crown in his hand. She will no longer be called Forsaken or Desolate but Hephzibah and Beulah, because the LORD delights in her and her land will be married. Watchmen are set on Jerusalem's walls to pray without rest until the LORD establishes her as a praise on the earth. The LORD swears that her grain and wine will no longer go to enemies and foreigners, and the people are told to prepare the highway and raise a banner because salvation and reward are coming. The chapter ends with new names for the people: The Holy People, The LORD's Redeemed, and Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: Zion is the one for whose sake the speaker will not keep silent until her righteousness shines like the dawn. She is promised a new name, a place as a crown of beauty in the LORD's hand, and the end of being called Forsaken. She is also called "daughter of Zion" and told that her salvation comes.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: Jerusalem is the city for whose sake the speaker will not rest, and on whose walls the LORD has set watchmen. Those who call on the LORD are to give him no rest until he makes Jerusalem a praise on the earth. She is finally to be called "Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken."

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: The LORD will name Zion with a new name, holds her as a crown and royal diadem, and delights in her, rejoicing over her as a bridegroom over his bride. He swears by his right hand and the arm of his strength that her grain and new wine will no longer go to enemies and foreigners. He proclaims to the end of the earth that her salvation comes, with his reward and recompense with him.

l: watchmen (Jerusalem's watchmen), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: The LORD has set watchmen on Jerusalem's walls. They will never be silent day or night, and those who call on the LORD are urged to take no rest and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem as a praise on the earth.

l: salvation, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: Zion's salvation is compared to a burning lamp that shines out. The LORD proclaims to the end of the earth that Zion's salvation comes, with his reward and recompense accompanying it.

l: marriage (Zion's marriage imagery), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 62
s: Marriage imagery describes Zion's restoration: her land will be married, and her sons will marry her as a young man marries a virgin. The LORD will rejoice over her as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, and she receives the names Hephzibah and Beulah in place of Forsaken and Desolate.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 63
s: Chapter 63 opens with a dialogue in which a figure coming from Edom and Bozrah, with garments stained red, declares himself mighty to save; he says he trod the peoples alone in his anger as the day of vengeance and the year of his redeemed arrived. The speaker then recounts the LORD's loving kindnesses to the house of Israel, whom he called his people and became their Savior, sharing in their affliction and carrying them. Israel rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, so he became their enemy, yet he remembered the days of Moses and the leading through the sea and wilderness. The chapter ends with a prayer asking the LORD to look down from heaven, to show his zeal and compassion, and to return for his servants' sake, since he is their Father and Redeemer. The people lament that adversaries have trodden down the sanctuary and that they have become like those never ruled by him.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 63
s: The LORD is portrayed as the one who comes from Edom in blood-stained garments, having trodden the wine press alone in anger and wrath, with no one to help, and whose own arm brought salvation. He is also recalled as the Savior of Israel who was afflicted in their affliction, redeemed and carried them, then turned against them when they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit. The people appeal to him as Father and Redeemer from everlasting, asking him to look down, show his zeal and compassion, and return.

l: Israel (the people), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 63
s: Israel is called the LORD's people, children who would not deal falsely, and he saved, redeemed and carried them in the days of old, including through the sea and wilderness under Moses. They rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, so he became their enemy and fought against them. In the closing prayer they say Abraham and Israel do not know them, ask why they wander and have hardened hearts, and lament that their holy people held the land briefly, adversaries have trodden down the sanctuary, and they are like those never ruled by him.

l: peoples (the LORD's enemies), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 63
s: The peoples are those the LORD trod down alone in his anger and wrath, trampling them like grapes in a wine press so that their lifeblood sprinkled his garments. He made them drunk in his wrath and poured their lifeblood out on the earth, and no one from among them was with him.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: In Chapter 64 the speakers plead with the LORD to tear the heavens and come down, so that the mountains quake and the nations tremble before his name as they did when he did awesome things they did not expect. They affirm that no one has ever seen a God besides him who works for those who wait for him. They confess that the LORD was angry and they sinned, that they have all become unclean, that their righteousness is like a polluted garment, and that their iniquities carry them away like the wind. They appeal to the LORD as Father and potter, with themselves as clay and the work of his hand, and ask him not to be furious or remember iniquity forever. They lament that the holy cities, Zion, Jerusalem and the burned house where their fathers praised him are wasted, and ask whether he will stay silent and punish them severely.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: The LORD is asked to tear the heavens and come down, make his name known to his adversaries, and not be furious or remember iniquity forever. He is described as having done awesome things unexpectedly, as a God unlike any other who works for those who wait for him, and as one who met those who do righteousness. He was angry, hid his face from the speakers and consumed them by means of their iniquities, and is addressed as Father and potter. The chapter ends with the speakers asking whether he will hold back, stay silent and punish them very severely.

l: we (the speakers), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: The speakers confess that they sinned and have been in sin a long time, that they are all like one unclean, and that their righteousness is like a polluted garment. They fade like a leaf and are carried off by their iniquities, and none calls on God's name or stirs himself to take hold of him. They appeal to the LORD as their Father, call themselves clay and the work of his hand and his people, and ask whether they shall be saved.

l: Zion, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: Zion is said to have become a wilderness. It is named among the holy cities that lie desolate.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: Jerusalem is described as a desolation. It is lamented together with Zion and the other holy cities that have become a wilderness.

l: house (our holy and beautiful house), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: The speakers call it the holy and beautiful house where their fathers praised the LORD. It is now burned with fire, and all their pleasant places are laid waste.

l: sin and iniquity, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: The speakers say they sinned when the LORD was angry and have been in sin a long time. Their iniquities carry them away like the wind, and the LORD has consumed them by means of these iniquities. They ask the LORD not to remember iniquity forever.

l: God's descent and awesome deeds, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 64
s: The speakers beg the LORD to tear the heavens and come down so that mountains quake and nations tremble, as when fire kindles brushwood and makes water boil. They recall that he came down before, did awesome things they did not look for, and the mountains quaked at his presence. They say no one from of old has heard of, perceived or seen a God besides him who works for those who wait for him.

l: The Book of Isaiah, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: In this chapter the LORD speaks of a rebellious people who provoke him with idolatrous sacrifices, burning incense on bricks and mountains, sitting among graves, eating pig's meat, and claiming to be holier than others. He promises to repay their iniquities and those of their fathers, and to destine those who forsake him and prepare a table for Fortune and Destiny to the sword. He will spare a remnant, bringing offspring out of Jacob and Judah, so that his chosen servants inherit his mountains while Sharon and the valley of Achor become places for flocks and herds. The LORD contrasts his servants, who will eat, drink, rejoice and be called by another name, with the wicked, who will hunger, thirst, wail and leave their name as a curse. He then announces the creation of new heavens and a new earth and of Jerusalem as a delight, where weeping ends, lives are long, labor is not in vain, prayers are answered before they are spoken, and the wolf and lamb feed together on his holy mountain.

l: the LORD, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: The LORD says he was found by those who did not seek him and spread out his hands all day to a rebellious people. He vows to repay their iniquities, destine those who forsake him to the sword, and spare a remnant for his servants' sake. He announces that he creates new heavens, a new earth and Jerusalem as a delight, and promises to answer before his people call.

l: rebellious people, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: They are described as walking in a way that is not good, provoking the LORD to his face by sacrificing in gardens, burning incense on bricks and mountains, sitting among graves, eating pig's meat, and saying they are holier than others. They forsake the LORD and prepare a table for Fortune and Destiny, and are told they will be destined to the sword because they did not answer when he called. They will leave their name as a curse to his chosen.

l: servants of the LORD (my servants), The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: The LORD spares them as one saves new wine found in a cluster, bringing offspring out of Jacob and Judah to inherit his mountains and dwell there. They will eat, drink, rejoice and sing for joy while the wicked suffer, and will be called by another name. They will build and inhabit houses, plant and eat from vineyards, enjoy long lives, and not labor in vain.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: The LORD says he will create Jerusalem to be a delight and her people a joy. He will rejoice in Jerusalem and delight in his people, and the voice of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her.

l: new heavens and new earth, The Book of Isaiah, Chapter 65
s: The LORD declares that he creates new heavens and a new earth, and the former things will not be remembered or come into mind. His people are told to be glad and rejoice forever in what he creates. It is paired with a peaceable holy mountain where wolf and lamb feed together and nothing hurts or destroys.
